query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a thin, continuous alumina (Al2O3) surface layer on the boride-based component will improve its resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based component with its native, unmodified surface.
generation.intervention: Expose the component surface to a controlled oxygen environment at elevated temperature (pre-oxidation) to induce the formation of a protective alumina scale.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed prior to exposure to molten aluminum, at temperatures that favor alumina formation without excessive oxidation of the bulk material. The protective effect is expected to persist during hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (i.e., high temperatures in an oxygen-lean molten aluminum bath) where the alumina scale remains adherent and chemically stable.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, dense, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) layer acting as a diffusion barrier between the molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed alumina scale hinders the direct contact of the corrosive molten aluminum with the underlying boride, thus reducing elemental dissolution and slowing down the corrosion kinetics. This barrier minimizes mass loss compared to untreated surfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components receiving the pre-oxidation treatment will show significantly lower mass loss and surface degradation when immersed in molten aluminum, compared to an untreated, native boride surface.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components with their as-fabricated, untreated surfaces typically experience higher rates of molten-aluminum induced corrosion due to direct exposure and lack of a protective barrier.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the alumina scale is expected to depend on maintaining its integrity; extreme deviations in operating temperature, overly reducing environments, or mechanical wear that disrupts the scale may compromise its protective ability.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thickness and microstructure of the alumina scale required for optimal protection on boride surfaces are not yet well established. There is some uncertainty regarding the scale’s long-term adherence under dynamic plating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based component samples. Treat one set with the controlled pre-oxidation process designed to form an alumina layer, while the other set is left untreated. Expose both sets to molten aluminum under identical plating conditions (temperature, exposure time, and environment).
measurements: Quantitative mass loss measurements before and after exposure.
Surface microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, XRD) to evaluate the presence and integrity of the alumina layer.
Corrosion rate assessment via cross-sectional analysis.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion (i.e., lower mass loss and improved surface integrity) compared to the untreated controls, or if the alumina layer is found to degrade rapidly under the test conditions, then the hypothesis that the pre-oxidation intervention improves molten-aluminum corrosion resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6
